item.title: Understanding End-of-Life Concerns for the Elderly
item.description:
End-of-life care is when someone is caring for another person during the last month or weeks of their life. Understanding end of life care can be helpful for the family to know what to expect. It creates a plan for those who are approaching the end of their life and revolves around the needs of the person as a whole. End-of-life concerns typically focus on making sure there are no tasks that haven’t been taken care of after the individual has passed.

End-of-life concerns revolve around the comfort and physical needs of the person. However, learning to manage the emotions of the family members is also an important aspect of end-of-life care.

Types of Care

There are a few types of care given during times of illness depending on the illness and its prognosis.

End-of-life care focuses on the process a person goes through as they approach the end of their life. This type of care focuses on the whole person, including their mental and spiritual selves.

Palliative care is simply controlling pain to improve a person’s quality of life and can be given at any time during a person’s illness.

Curative care is care given to cure the illness.

Hospice care is for those individuals who are terminally ill and is focused on controlling pain and other symptoms.

Signs of End-of-Life

Just as each individual is unique, so also will their death experiences be. For some, it may be a slow process, while others will experience a quick transition to death. It is important to remember that regardless of how it progresses, each person needs to have comfort and dignity during this time.

End-of-life concerns typically include the presence of someone near them just for soothing conversations and acts of compassion. End of life can come in stages as outlined below.
Months (40-90 days)
Loss of Appetite: As a person nears the end of life, it is normal for them to have a loss of appetite. As a result, there is a weight loss.

Fatigue and Weakness: The body is starting to slow down so this can lead to an increased desire to sleep. Because the body is not getting fuel through food, it will start to become weak. This means that movement is difficult for the person.

Withdrawing from People: When death is becoming a realization, the person may start to withdraw. They will start separating from friends and family. There may also be times of reflection on life and regrets.

Discussions about Death: Individuals will talk openly about end-of-life wishes. Faith and cultural backgrounds play an important role in how a person views death.

Pain: Pain is a common symptom that may vary for each person. It may come from the illness, or it could be a result of emotional distress.

Nausea: Nausea can result from different reasons. Constipation, medications, or emotional stress can contribute to nausea.
Weeks before the End of Life:
Eating may stop It is a normal process for eating to stop due to lack of appetite. This is a normal process and does not speed up the end-of-life process.

Restlessness Medicine and chemical changes in the brain can lead to restlessness and agitation. This may result in senseless movements.

Confusion During this time, the respiratory system provides less oxygen to the brain, and this can cause confusion and delirium.

Hallucinations Seeing or hearing things or people that are not there is common during the last weeks or days of life.

Increased Sleep It is not uncommon for a person to sleep most of the day when nearing the end of life. They may even sleep for a few days before seeming to be awake. They will typically respond if someone attempts to wake them.

Skin Color Change Due to the change in circulation, the person’s hands, feet, and knees may be discolored, purple, or grey. They can also have areas of dark blotchy patches (mottled skin) on their back.

Labored Breathing Being self-active means that a person needs less oxygen. Because of this, a person facing end of life will have breathing that is shallow and less frequent.

Incontinence For individuals facing the end of life, it’s not unusual for them to lose control of their bladder or bowels. Typically, their bathroom needs are reduced as they are not eating and drinking normally.
Days before the End of Life
Unconsciousness and Unresponsive As the end-of-life approaches, the sleep pattern of the person may increase to the point that there is little consciousness. When there is an attempt to wake them, they may be unresponsive.

Irregular Vital Signs It is not uncommon for vital signs to be irregular. This includes blood pressure, heart rate, and body temperature.

Cessation of Eating or Drinking As they are near the end of life, a person may come to a point where they are unable to eat due to gastrointestinal issues or choking.

Restlessness There may be a period of restlessness or agitation for these individuals. As they draw nearer to death, they may not recognize those around them.
Hours before the End of Life
Breathing Changes Most of the time people nearing the end of life will exhibit Cheyne Stokes breathing. This breathing pattern cycles from a gradual increase in breathing followed by a decrease. There is also a period where sleep apnea is present. This cycle will continue because the body is trying to recover from the change in carbon dioxide levels.

Pain There are times when some individuals will show signs of being in pain. They may even grimace or cry out. Pain management can be planned through the healthcare team.

Skin, Body Fluid, and Breath Odor As they near death, there are metabolism changes that cause skin, body fluids, and breath to smell similar to acetone.

Noisy Breathing Eventually, the breathing will become loud and congested. This comes from the inability to reabsorb fluids in the throat or chest.

Cold Extremities (Hands, Feet, Nose, and Ears) Compromised circulation will also cause these areas to feel cold to the touch.

End-of-Life Concerns

To promote a peaceful process for end of life, there must be ground rules in place. Having compassion amid a trying time can ensure that all involved will find the support needed to adjust to the transition and loss.

As humans, we can be harsh during the hard times of losing someone dear to us. Some decisions need to be made but are not well thought out because of the emotional and mental distress of death. For this reason, it is best to make sure there are agreements and rules for behavior to ensure that your loved one isn’t surrounded by arguments during the last days of life.

Talking to other family members can help with navigating fears about death. This should be done before the passing of the loved one. There are many ways to find help with this issue. Christian counselors, books, and pastors are great avenues of support and information.

The most important end-of-life concern is that you honor the wishes that the dying individual has put into place. This will reduce the stress of decision-making and allow you to grieve healthily. Honoring your loved one isn’t just about carrying out their wishes regarding details for services and execution of the will.

Honoring them means you are taking care of yourself, doing good things in their name, starting new chapters in life, remembering to be joyful, and showing others grace in the middle of grief.

Getting Support

It is normal to have end-of-life concerns when facing death. It is terrifying to imagine life without a loved one. You begin to grieve even before the person has passed. Caring for a dying person is also emotionally strenuous. Consider reaching out to a counselor to walk you through the process. Feel free to contact our offices today and we can connect you with a Christian therapist who is skillful at navigating grief, death, and supporting the dying.

item.title: Breaking Out of the Sleep Anxiety Spiral
item.description:
Some people get to a certain age, and they realize that they have been exhausted for months or even years. Sleep loss affects an array of people, from teens in the middle of exams, new parents adjusting to the demands of an infant, or elderly people dealing with rapid changes in their lives. Some people are simply tired because events like these are demanding, but many people are tired because they have sleep anxiety.

Sleep anxiety is not the same as insomnia; it is the things that cause insomnia. It is the fear you start to feel as bedtime nears, as you worry that you will not fall asleep. It is the dread you feel when you wake up in the middle of the night and see that it is only midnight. You spend hours in bed, willing yourself to sleep, but failing. You can’t help but think about your day tomorrow and the consequences of losing sleep.

Sleep anxiety is debilitating, but it can be fixed without medication or substances. Studies have shown that medication does not help with sleep anxiety in the long-term. When you begin to understand what is going on in your head and in your body, you will begin to unpack some of the anxiety surrounding your sleep problems, breaking the sleep anxiety spiral. Your overthinking might be the thing driving your sleep anxiety, but your mind is also the solution.

The Sleep Anxiety Spiral

The most frustrating thing about sleep anxiety is that it is self-perpetuating. You stress about not being able to fall asleep or stay asleep, and it is that stress that causes sleeplessness. It is like being so afraid of failing your driving test that you cannot concentrate and end up failing the test. It is a form of self-fulfilling prophecy.

Sleep anxiety doesn’t only cause you stress in the evenings, but it also affects your daytime routine. Many people believe that they can only function properly on eight solid hours of sleep per day. This is a common idea that intensifies sleep anxiety. It looks like this: you believe that you need eight hours of quality sleep per day, and so you become anxious that you won’t get that. Then it is your anxiety over not getting enough sleep that becomes the very thing preventing you from getting enough sleep.

There are things you can do and things you must keep from doing to break the sleep anxiety spiral. Overall, you must change your approach to sleep, change the way you think about sleep, and make some changes to your routine. By interrupting your thoughts and behavior this way, you are creating a new pattern for yourself, and it can adapt to your new lifestyle.

Things You Must Do to Interrupt Sleep Anxiety

There are several practical things that you can start doing to interrupt the sleep anxiety spiral. It is a good idea to speak with a doctor or specialist before starting this new regimen, or with anyone who can keep you accountable and provide support. These ideas range from simple tips to deeper and broader attitude changes.

Firstly, create a healthy bedtime routine and stick to it. Your body has a function called the circadian rhythm. This is a set of automatic responses that your central nervous system performs throughout the day to help you. When your brain registers that it is nearing bedtime, it will release a hormone called melatonin into your nervous system. This hormone brings down your cortisol levels, puts your bladder and bowels on pause for the night, and generally prepares your body to be inactive for the next eight to ten hours.

You can help your circadian rhythm in practical ways by following a 3-2-1 principle. Have your final meal of the night three hours before bedtime, have your final drink two hours before bedtime, and reduce screen time for the last hour before bed. This will prime your body for sleep even if your mind is overactive.

With sleep anxiety, you struggle to fall asleep, and you struggle to stay asleep. The first thing most people do when they wake up is to look at the clock and calculate how many hours of sleep they have left. Try taking away your ability to time-check. Remove clocks from your bedroom and place your phone far away from your bedside. This interrupts the compulsive time-checking and the anxiety that comes with it.

In a larger sense, you must change the way you think about sleeping. For example, you might believe that you can only function during the day if you have had more than six hours of sleep the night before.

The truth is that you can be perfectly functional on minimal sleep, even over a long period of time. New parents experience years of sleeplessness and still manage to get by successfully. Sometimes it is your internal beliefs about sleep that contribute the most to sleep anxiety.

Lean into the idea that you are going to be tired tomorrow, and that it’s okay. Accept whatever amount of sleep you get, whether it’s only a few solid hours. Think of nighttime as rest time rather than sleep time.

The fact that you are lying down in a relaxed, safe environment and not looking at screens is enough for your body; sleep would be a bonus. When you change the way you think about sleep, sleep anxiety begins to lose its footing and influence over your mind.

Things to Avoid While Dealing with Sleep Anxiety

It’s natural to feel helpless and overwhelmed with sleep anxiety, and many people resort to using medication and substances like alcohol to cope. These things might help get you some sleep occasionally, but there is a real danger of becoming dependent on them over time. If you have been using medication or substances to help with sleep anxiety, aim to stop using them entirely.

Avoiding screen time before bed and keeping clocks out of sight is good, but it’s also a good idea to get up if you wake up at a certain time. When you lie in bed chasing sleep, you tend to begin overthinking and stressing.

You could try using mindfulness techniques or tools like brain shuffling to get back to sleep, but it’s a better idea to get up and go to a quiet spot in the house for some reading or crafting. Try to avoid screens still, and it’s best not to eat or drink anything. Instead, doing a relaxed activity in a dimly lit room will help keep the anxiety at bay. Eventually, you will become sleepy again, at which point you can simply return to bed to sleep.

Many sleep-tracking apps try to address insomnia, but these have the opposite effect on sleep anxiety. When you have a visualization for how much sleep you’re not getting, that intensifies the anxiety you feel. The goal is to be rested, not to get the perfect amount of sleep each night. Avoid tracking your sleep or trying to meet sleep goals. Instead, aim to have a restful evening. If you fall asleep for a few hours, that’s great. If you don’t, it’s not the end of the world.

Sleep anxiety is difficult, but it’s a cycle you can break. It might not happen overnight, but if you can get to a place where you feel more rested and less anxious, you will have made incredible progress. Give yourself a break because you deserve it.

Some things are easier to face and overcome with someone on your side. Consider meeting with a counselor if your sleep anxiety has become overwhelming. If you don’t have a counselor, we hope that you can find someone suitable in our online catalog or by enlisting the help of our reception team.

item.title: Depression in Women: What to Know and What to Do
item.description:
Women are more likely to develop depression than men due to many factors. This can leave a woman feeling a loss of self-esteem and confidence in her abilities, and wondering if the feeling of emptiness will ever subside.

The good news is that depression is a treatable mental condition. However, depression in women must be treated early before symptoms become severe. Recognizing the symptoms and becoming aware of what to do to alleviate the effects can help you overcome depression and regain control of your life.

Why Women are More Likely to Develop Depression

Depression in women is more likely due to several factors.

Genetics and family history can play a role in whether a woman develops depression. She may be more genetically “hard-wired” for feeling down, or she grew up in a household with someone who struggled with the mental condition.

Chemical imbalances can worsen depression symptoms or create coexisting mental conditions, such as anxiety disorders. The effects of trauma or abuse can trigger depression that can last weeks, months, or years without treatment.

Consult with your physician about the side effects of any medications you currently take, as the side effects of several can lower mood and lead to depression and anxiety.

Symptoms of Depression in Women

Familiarizing yourself with the symptoms of depression in women can help you know when to seek treatment. If you have had symptoms for more than two weeks, speak to a counselor. Some mental conditions, such as bipolar disorder, cycle through manic and depressive episodes that repeat for months or years. Don’t continue to suffer from depression. Learn the symptoms and seek help.

Sadness – Persistent sadness that doesn’t go away and lasts for two or more weeks. Sadness is a hallmark of depression and can appear as mild to severe.

Fatigue – A bone-weariness that makes it difficult to go about your typical day. You may want to stay in bed or find it challenging to keep up with personal hygiene and housework.

Mood swings – Irritability and sudden mood swings make it challenging for others to live and work in your space. You may experience crying jags.

Feeling guilt or shame – You may experience feelings of guilt or shame. These feelings can be due to something from your past, a worry about the future, or trauma. You may feel guilty for missing out on your child’s school event due to depression.

Trouble concentrating – Depression affects cognitive function. You may have trouble concentrating or focusing on tasks. You may forget small or large details or dates. This forgetfulness and lack of focus can interfere with your work and the goals you have set.

Changes in appetite – You may notice changes in your appetite. Depression can alter ghrelin and leptin, the hormones responsible for hunger and satiety. This can lead to rapid weight gain or loss.

Changes in sleep – Adrenaline, cortisol, and other stress hormones can interfere with quality sleep. You may sleep too much, partly due to fatigue, or have trouble falling and staying asleep. It is common for people struggling with depression to feel tired but unable to sleep.

Headaches – Headaches, stomachaches, and unexplained body aches are common with depression in women. You may also notice a change in your menstrual cycle due to the combination of depression and hormonal fluctuations.

Substance abuse – Substance abuse can worsen depression symptoms, yet many people choose alcohol or drugs to numb the pain or to feel something other than the numbness or emptiness that can accompany depression. Substance abuse can lead to addiction, which may require the help of a mental health professional to break the cycle.

Suicidal thoughts – Intrusive thoughts, urges to self-harm, and suicidal ideations can develop with depression if left untreated. If you or a loved one is experiencing any of these, seek help immediately.

Don’t continue to suffer from depression. Learn the symptoms and seek help. Christian counseling can help draw you closer to God and His Son, Jesus Christ, while learning the strategies to overcome depression. You can feel joy again through and in Him.

What to Do for Depression in Women

Although professional treatment is often required to break free from depression, there are lifestyle changes you can make to alleviate symptoms. The goal is to resume daily activities and break the cycle of negative thoughts and emotions. It is a combination of a healthier lifestyle, counseling, and treatments, such as Cognitive Behavioral Therapy, that can help you reach the other side.

Seek treatment

No amount of lifestyle changes can overcome severe depression in women. They can help to boost mood and set the body on the correct course toward healing, but treatment through a mental health care practitioner can really make the difference.

When you combine Christian counseling with psychological methods geared toward depression, your care plan addresses both body and mind. You cover the physical, emotional, mental, and spiritual areas of your life. You learn to adopt new strategies to manage depression while leaning into the Great Physician for grace and healing.

Get more active

Becoming more active can suppress the sympathetic nervous system and activate the parasympathetic nervous system. The release of endorphins and serotonin can leave you happier, more confident, and calmer. When you engage in heart-pumping exercise, these endorphins calm the fight-or-flight response.

Consider adding 20 to 30 minutes of exercise to your daily routine. Try to vary your workouts. For example, take a brisk walk on Monday, lift weights on Tuesday, practice Pilates on Wednesday, and meet friends for a swim at the pool on Thursday.

Ditch inflammatory foods

Inflammatory foods worsen depression symptoms. Ultra-processed, packaged foods, and foods high in salt and fat can contribute to chronic inflammation, which increases your risk for other conditions as well, including high blood pressure, high cholesterol, stroke, heart attack, Type 2 diabetes, and obesity.

A nutritionist can review your current daily diet and recommend healthier swaps that might boost your mood. Stick to leaner cuts of meat, healthier fats, whole grains, and fresh fruits and vegetables. Try to avoid packaged and processed foods, or any food high in sugar or salt.

Practice stress management

Stress contributes to depression, anxiety, and a host of other mental and physical conditions. Chronic stress also triggers inflammation, which can make you physically and mentally ill. To combat this, practice stress management as part of your daily routine. Instead of waiting until you feel bad, incorporate activities into your daily habits.

For example, take the time in the morning to rub lotion or cream into your skin after bathing. The act of massaging skin can help calm and focus your mind on the present. Try spreading activities throughout the day and week.

Perhaps spend two minutes practicing deep breathing every afternoon and curling up in a chair to read a good book every Thursday evening. Give yourself a pleasurable activity daily and weekly to make you feel good.

Build a support system

A support system can include friends, family, or acquaintances who are familiar with depression in women. Having a support system can keep you accountable.

These people can check on you when you find yourself isolating from the world. They can stop by your home, ask how you are feeling, and encourage you to participate in social functions. Choose people who will listen when you need them and be there for you when you struggle.

Virtual Christian Counseling for Depression

As a Christian woman, you were meant to live a life of purpose and calling. Depression can rob you of the will to move forward. Seek help if depression interferes with your life.

Contact our reception team today to connect with a Christian counselor specializing in depression in women. We also offer virtual counseling sessions to accommodate your schedule. Call us today to schedule an appointment.

item.title: Is Inattentive ADHD the Reason Your Teen No Longer Believes in Themselves?
item.description:
You know your teen. You see the way they light up when they talk about something they love. You’ve watched them take pride when they do well, whether it’s a good grade, a creative idea, or a kind gesture. But lately, your teen seems more withdrawn.

They shrug off praise, avoid challenges, and seem convinced they’ll fail before they even start. It’s heartbreaking to watch, especially when you know how much potential they have. Even when you try to remind them that they’re smart and capable, they don’t seem to believe you anymore.

Sometimes, this loss of confidence isn’t just emotional; it’s connected to how their brain processes focus and attention. Inattentive ADHD can slowly affect how a teen sees themselves, even when no one realizes it’s there. For many adolescents, inattentive ADHD plays a bigger role than most people realize.

Why Inattentive ADHD Feeds Self-Doubt

Inattentive ADHD does not manifest in the stereotypical way most people would expect with ADHD. There’s no bouncing off the walls or constant blurting out of words. Instead, it’s the kind that makes a teen drift off mid-task, forget instructions quickly, lose track of time, or miss basic details. It’s a unique kind of ADHD that’s not easy to spot until it starts affecting how they see themselves.

Your teen might be smart, thoughtful, and creative. If they constantly forget homework, zone out during lectures, or struggle to stay organized, they start to feel like they’re failing at things that seem easy for everyone else.

When that happens again and again, it doesn’t just frustrate them; it chips away at their confidence. Eventually, they don’t just think they’re bad at school but that they’re bad at being themselves.

How You Know Something Has Changed in Your Teen’s Self-Image

A young person’s confidence doesn’t disappear all at once. Typically, it fades bit by bit in ways you may not even notice if you’re not looking closely.

You might see your teen:

  • Avoiding group projects or leadership roles they used to enjoy.
  • Giving up on hobbies they once loved.
  • Getting defensive when you try to encourage them.
  • Saying “I’m not good at anything” more than they used to.
  • Hesitating to try new things, even when they’re interesting.

Many times, those aren’t just personality changes, but might be signs that your teen is questioning their worth. If a condition like inattentive ADHD is part of the picture, those doubts come from a place of repeated frustration, not a lack of effort.

What Doesn’t Help (Even If It Sounds Supportive)

Sometimes, encouragement backfires. Phrases like “You’re so smart, you just need to apply yourself” or “You have so much potential” can feel like pressure. They remind your teen of everything they’re not living up to. When they’re already feeling defeated, those words don’t lift them; they weigh them down.

Other things that tend to make things worse:

  • Comparing them to siblings or classmates.
  • Overloading them with reminders or checklists.
  • Assuming they are being purposely defiant when they forget something.
  • Expecting them to “grow out of it” without support.

These responses don’t come from a place of harm. But they miss the mark when it comes to what your teen needs. They reinforce the idea that their struggles are personal failures, not signs that their brains work differently.

The Problem with Saying “Just Try Harder”

Before you assume it’s just teenage mood swings, consider whether inattentive ADHD is part of what’s making them lose faith in their own abilities. It’s tempting to respond with advice. “You just need to focus.” “You have to be more responsible.” “You’re capable, you just need to apply yourself.”

But for teens dealing with such a unique condition, those words don’t help. Instead, they reinforce the idea that the problem is a personal flaw, not a brain-based challenge. So, when adults repeat those messages, even with good intentions, teens start to internalize them.

Rather than feeling supported, they feel judged. Instead of learning tools that work for their brain, they’re told to push through with strategies that don’t. That disconnect makes them feel misunderstood, and then it’s hard to build confidence when they don’t feel seen.

Why This Feels Personal to Your Teen

Teens are already trying to figure out who they are. They’re building their identity, testing their strengths, and learning how to handle setbacks. When inattentive ADHD keeps tripping them up, it doesn’t just frustrate them; it makes them question their place in the world.

They start to wonder:

  • “Why do I forget things no matter how hard I try?”
  • “Why does everyone think I’m lazy when I’m trying my best?”
  • “Why do I feel behind even when I’m working all the time?”

These questions aren’t just academic. They’re emotional. They determine how your teen sees themselves, and whether they believe they’re capable of succeeding.

What Helps Confidence Grow Again

Confidence isn’t built by fixing everything at once. It’s built by helping your teen feel capable in small, consistent ways. Here are a few approaches that make a real difference:

Focus on effort, not outcome Instead of praising perfect results, notice when your teen tries something hard, sticks with a task, or asks for help. That kind of encouragement builds resilience.

Use tools that match their brain Timers, visual schedules, and short task lists can help teens with inattentive ADHD stay on track without feeling overwhelmed. Let them experiment with what works best.

Let them teach you something Give them space to share what they know, whether it’s about a video game, a book, or a random fact. When they feel respected, their confidence grows.

Reframe forgetfulness as a signal, not a failure If your teen forgets something, treat it as a clue that their system needs adjusting, not as proof they’re careless.

Give them space to reset Sometimes, teens with inattentive ADHD need a break before they can re-engage. Let them pause without guilt. It helps them come back with more clarity.

Ask what support feels helpful Instead of guessing, ask your teen what kind of help makes things easier. You might be surprised by what they say.

Starting the Conversation About Getting Help

If you’re wondering how to bring up counseling or an evaluation, start small. Teens respond best when they feel respected, not corrected. You could say something like, “I’ve noticed school feels harder lately. Would you be open to talking with someone who understands this better?” Keep the tone calm and curious rather than urgent. Let them know counseling isn’t about confirming that something is wrong with them; it’s about giving them tools to make life easier.

You can also share stories of people who’ve found support through therapy or diagnosis, which helps normalize the idea. Offer choices: “Would you rather talk to someone online or in person?” When teens feel ownership of the decision, they’re more likely to agree. The right conversation can be the start of real healing.

As a parent, you also deserve support. You don’t have to figure this out alone. Counseling can help you respond in ways that build connection instead of conflict. It can help you understand what’s going on beneath the surface and give you strategies that truly work.

Teens with inattentive ADHD benefit from counseling that helps them understand how their brains work and how to work with them. Therapy can give both you and them language for what they’re experiencing, tools to manage frustration, and a space to rebuild their confidence without judgment.

If you’re seeing signs that your teen is losing confidence and you suspect inattentive ADHD is part of the picture, don’t wait. Book a session with a teen therapist listed on this site or call us and speak to a representative today.

item.title: Understanding the Types of BPD and Their Connection to Substance Abuse
item.description:
Borderline personality disorder (BPD) affects how individuals experience themselves and relate to the world around them. Seeking relief from the emotional intensity that comes with BPD, individuals sometimes turn to substance abuse as a common coping mechanism. To understand why some people find themselves caught in patterns that they want to escape, we first have to understand the types of BPD and how they intersect with addiction.

There is a relationship between these two struggles that goes beyond a simple cause-and-effect. It reflects deeper questions about identity, managing pain, and a human need for stability. The way BPD manifests can determine not only how someone experiences their internal world, but which substances they turn to, and why. These distinctions are essential to break free from the cycle of emotional dysregulation and addiction.

Four Patterns Common Across the Multiple Types of BPD

Because each person is unique, borderline personality disorder doesn’t present the same way in everyone. Four primary patterns help explain the different ways that BPD manifests. These types of BPD are not meant to box people into categories concretely, but rather, they help us understand the ways emotional dysregulation shows up in real life. By recognizing which patterns resonate most with an individual, Christian counselors can guide treatment and offer hope that recovery is possible.

The discouraged type: This form of BPD often appears in people who seem dependent and seek constant reassurance while struggling with feelings of worthlessness. These individuals may appear passive or submissive in relationships and avoid confrontation, even when it would be healthy.

The impulsive type: Those who manifest this type of BPD often engage in risk-taking behaviors and emotional outbursts without concern for consequences. People who struggle with this form of BPT typically act on every feeling without pausing to consider the outcome, and they chase experiences that provide immediate gratification or distraction from inner emptiness.

The petulant type: This form of BPD involves stubborn negativity and feeling misunderstood, which results in pushing others away by simultaneously fearing abandonment. Individuals struggling with this pattern often feel like victims of their circumstances and may express bitterness or resentment toward those trying to help.

The self-destructive type: This pattern of BPD manifests in harmful behaviors directed inward, which include substance abuse, self-harm, or extreme risk-taking to manage unbearable emotional pain. Individuals of this type are the most visibly concerning. They seem intent on destroying themselves, even though self-harm isn’t about wanting to die. It’s about making internal pain visible.

Each of these patterns reflects a different strategy for managing the emotional dysregulation that is at the heart of BPD. Many individuals display characteristics from multiple types, and patterns can shift over time, so these categories are not considered rigid.

The consistency across these patterns is the intense fear of abandonment, unstable self-image, and difficulty regulating emotions that define the disorder. Adding substance abuse to this already intense struggle starts as an attempt to navigate the emotional turbulence that feels impossible to manage any other way.

Why Substance Abuse Co-Occurs with BPD

The connection between BPD and addiction is not coincidental. Most individuals diagnosed with BPD also struggle with substance use disorders. Because BPD creates an emotionally intense environment, substances often offer temporary relief from these struggles.

An individual experiencing rapid mood swings, chronic feelings of emptiness, and a fear of abandonment turns to alcohol or other substances to quiet the internal chaos. Substances only provide a brief escape from emotions that feel overwhelming and unmanageable.

Self-medication is not the only challenge with substance abuse and BPD. The brain chemistry is changed due to substance use, which can worsen BPD symptoms and create a cycle where each issue amplifies the other. Impulsivity is a core feature of BPD, and it can become more pronounced under the influence of substances, and emotional regulation becomes nearly impossible.

Christian counselors recognize that both conditions require integrated treatment. They emphasize that addressing one only leaves the underlying vulnerabilities untouched. The path to healing requires understanding how these struggles reinforce each other and learning how to cultivate healthier ways to cope with emotional pain. One good place to start is with encouraging Scriptures:

Cast your burden upon the Lord and He will sustain you; He will never allow the righteous to be shaken. – Psalm 55:22, NASB

How Different Types of BPD Influence Substance Use Patterns

A specific pattern of BPD often shapes the relationship an individual has with substances. Impulsive-type individuals engage in binge drinking or experiment with multiple substances, trying to find a thrill and temporary relief from boredom or inner emptiness.

Individuals who struggle with the self-destructive type of BPD may use substances deliberately to harm themselves or engage in dangerous combinations of risky behaviors. They are less concerned with pleasure and more focused on punishing themselves or numbing severe emotional pain.

Individuals who struggle with the discouraged type often use substances to cope with feelings of hopelessness and inadequacy. Using substances becomes an internal coping mechanism to numb the discouraging feelings.

The individual who suffers from the petulant type of BPD faces a more complex dynamic when it comes to substance use. They may engage in substance use in response to a perceived rejection or conflict. The result is a pattern where relationship struggles trigger substance use, which creates more relationship problems.

Christian counselors understand these patterns and can develop treatment approaches that address the specific needs of each individual who struggles with substance use and BPD. The goal is to build healthier ways to manage emotional experiences that made substances feel necessary in the first place.

Still, we are all reminded of Jesus’ words:

“Come to Me, all who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.” – Matthew 11:28, NASB

The Path Toward Integrated Healing

Co-occurring BPD and substance abuse recovery requires addressing both conditions simultaneously. If BPD remains untreated, traditional addiction treatment fails because the emotional dysregulation continues to drive the compulsion toward substances.

On the other hand, if BPD is treated without addressing active addiction, the treatment is ineffective because substances interfere with the ability to develop healthy coping strategies. Through integrated treatment, individuals learn to recognize that these conditions exist in relationship to one another and must be addressed together.

Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) has become an effective treatment plan for individuals dealing with both BPD and substance abuse. Through this approach, individuals learn specific skills to manage distress, tolerate stress, and build more effective relationships.

Christian counselors often integrate faith-based perspectives and evidence-based treatments to help clients understand their value in Christ as they develop practical tools to manage symptoms. This process involves learning that emotions do not have to be escaped or numbed. Even intense emotions can be experienced, understood, and regulated in healthy ways.

Finding the Support You Need

The relationship between BPD and substance abuse is a reflection of a human tendency to seek relief from pain through whatever feels available. For treatment to be effective, individuals must understand the different patterns of BPD and how they intersect with addiction.

Each type of BPD – the discouraged, the impulsive, the petulant, or the self-destructive – presents a unique challenge and strength in the recovery process. The consistency is the need for integrated treatment that addresses both the emotional dysregulation involved with BPD and addictive patterns.

Healthy recovery includes building new skills, developing healthier coping mechanisms, and discovering that lasting peace isn’t found by escaping emotions. Instead, you can learn to navigate feelings with grace, support, and God’s Word.

If you or someone you know is facing the complex challenges of BPD and substance abuse, professional support can make a meaningful difference in your recovery. Christian counselors are trained to integrate faith-based encouragement with evidence-based treatment to help you navigate this journey and find lasting recovery.

Reach out to our office and connect with a Christian counselor who can help you take the first step toward integrated care for these struggles.

item.title: The Smile that Hides Repressed Anger
item.description:
Sometimes anger can convince people that it’s not there. It doesn’t always come with a loud voice in a heated moment. It can roll in quietly, disguised as a tight jaw, sudden irritability, or a withdrawn spirit. Repressed anger is a deceptive emotion that many people carry.

By the time it’s recognized, it’s been living under the surface for months, and it no longer feels like anger. It has been shaping decisions and relationships for months or even years in ways that are hard to trace back to the source. Scripture has clear guidelines on anger:

In your anger do not sin: Do not let the sun go down while you are still angry. – Ephesians 4:26, NIV

The Bible tells us that we will experience anger, but it’s what we do in that anger that creates the struggles and issues. Repressed anger is deeper than a spiritual choice. Managing anger by keeping it out of sight and holding it at a distance can be the underlying assumption in faith communities. But now we are coming to understand that this is not handling it well and that the hidden anger carries real weight.

What Repressed Anger Really Looks Like

Repressed anger doesn’t identify itself by a name. It tends to present as persistent, low-grade sadness or unexplained irritability. It could be a withdrawal from once meaningful relationships.

This surfaces when people have spent years managing emotional responses for the sake of others, leading them to lose touch with what they’re actually feeling beneath the surface. By the time the anger surfaces, it may have been buried so long that the person no longer recognizes it for what it is.

Each individual has a choice to establish internal honesty. It’s not comfortable, but it is necessary for understanding how we manage emotional responses. In places that feel complicated or unflattering, an individual can begin to know themselves fully. Faith communities tend to suggest that certain emotions make self-examination a spiritual risk.

When individuals or communities have framed anger as a sign of spiritual immaturity or something that a truly trusting person doesn’t experience, honesty becomes difficult to access. Just because an emotion isn’t acknowledged doesn’t mean it disappears. It just learns to live quietly until it can’t anymore.

Search me, God, and know my heart; test me and know my anxious thoughts. See if there is any offensive way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting. – Psalm 139:23-24, NIV

The Hidden Cost of Keeping the Peace

Sometimes peace is a cover for avoidance, wearing a spiritual name. This happens when it involves staying quiet even though something genuinely needs to be said or moving past a wound before it has been addressed honestly. Surface-level peacemaking results in something that looks like patience but functions like suppression. The result is a calm exterior that pushes down everything that’s never been allowed to be named.

Anger does not have to be dissolved before it is examined to show emotional maturity. Wisdom in handling emotions comes from understanding the difference between unrestrained anger and engaging with what has been building beneath the surface.

Christian counselors help individuals who have chosen suppression over engagement, or who have lived under the belief that burying difficult emotions was the faithful choice. The process of understanding repressed anger begins with realizing that it does not protect a person. It only delays what will need to be addressed at a greater cost.

Repressed Anger and the Body’s Honest Response

Emotional suppression and physical health have a well-documented connection, especially when it comes to anger. The body will respond over time when anger has been withheld rather than processed. It shows up in chronic muscle tension, recurring headaches, digestive difficulties, and disrupted sleep.

The body was not created to absorb what the mind refuses to examine. It will register what is carried and communicate it in ways that become increasingly hard to ignore as the body reveals hidden issues through outward symptoms.

God’s Word offers straightforward instruction to be slow to anger, but there is a deeper meaning in this instruction than first appears. When an individual is slowed to anger, they adopt a posture that reflects thoughtfulness, reflection, and a willingness to listen before reacting. This is the opposite of suppression, which bypasses reflection entirely and buries the emotion without engagement.

Christian counselors can help individuals focus on the intersection of faith and emotional health by helping clients distinguish between the responses of suppression and reflection. Suppression is not being slow to anger. It is avoidance. Whatever an individual consistently avoids will find other ways to make itself known, whether through physical symptoms, relationships, or behavior.

My dear brothers and sisters, take note of this: Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak and slow to become angry, because human anger does not produce the righteousness that God desires. – James 1:19-20, NIV

Finding Honest Ground Between Repressed Anger and Real Healing

When an individual moves away from the belief that their emotions are a spiritual problem and toward the understanding that the emotions carry spiritual information, they experience a meaningful shift. Anger often points to something real, even when it is buried. It indicates there was a boundary that was crossed, a wound that was minimized by others, or a loss that was never fully grieved.

Christian counselors recognize this shift and can help individuals name and grapple with the repressed anger that leads to an honest foundation where true healing can take place. Jesus never suggested that an offense be minimized or set aside.

He named it in a way that extends beyond interpersonal conflict. It reaches into the inner work of honestly acknowledging what has been dismissed or left untouched. Reconciliation requires honesty, whether it’s with oneself or with others.

The resolve to deal with what has been left unresolved isn’t a detour from faith, but rather wisdom in action. Many individuals find that their faith comes alive and is practical when they are honest about the repressed anger hidden beneath the surface.

Discover the Peace You Long For

People often smile when they don’t have the language or feel safe enough to do anything else. A smile is intended to be a reflection of wholeness that comes from the outward and inward life aligning. God’s Word does not ask people to perform emotionally. He invites them to genuine peace formed through honest engagement with Him in the reality of personal experience. This includes the parts that have been living quietly beneath the surface.

Jesus describes a peace that is not built on suppressing what is difficult, or on pretending that it’s not there. This peace comes to those who fully acknowledge what they carry. Those who are moving through the process of naming a long-buried emotion and following it to its source move into a place of honest healing. This isn’t a deficit of faith or the lack of it, but it can be how faith comes alive from the inside out.

Peace I leave with you; my peace I give you. I do not give to you as the world gives. Do not let your hearts be troubled and do not be afraid. – John 14:27, NIV

If you think you may struggle with repressed anger, you don’t have to suppress it any longer. You don’t have to navigate the journey of understanding that anger alone. Contact our office and speak with our reception team to make an appointment. They will connect you with support that will help you navigate mental health and faith honestly.

item.title: Infidelity: How It Feels to Be Cheated On
item.description:
If you’ve experienced infidelity in your marriage, you’re not alone. According to Wendy Wang, Director of Research at the Institute of Family Studies, 20% of men and 13% of women in the United States have cheated on their spouse. That’s a fairly high number.

When you account for the fact that this study only focused on married couples, not those in long-term relationships, the number is likely higher. Add to that people who’ve had non-sexual affairs, such as those who have engaged in online or emotional affairs, and the number grows.

To say that you’re not alone if you’ve been cheated on is not an understatement. And while these numbers are staggering and indicate a larger, broader spiritual and moral problem in our modern world, knowing that you’re not experiencing this on your own can be comforting. What do they say about misery loving company?

Of course, being part of a statistic is not particularly comforting, especially when that statistic represents a broken relationship. But knowing that others before you have gone through this very thing and have made it out in one, thriving piece should bring some comfort.

If you’re reading this and have experienced infidelity, you might be feeling a whole host of uncomfortable emotions and be grappling with how to communicate them to others. Or maybe you’re the one who strayed, and you can’t quite figure out why your spouse is reacting the way they are. Many people know the technical reasons affairs hurt.

The broken promises and the betrayals are there, but beyond those cognitive reasons lies a broken, beating heart. Those emotions, the feelings and fallout of an affair, are not quite as easy to understand or communicate as the concrete broken rules. Keep reading to discover how being cheated on really feels.

Your comfort is gone.

If you’ve been in a relationship for any length of time, it’s logical to think that your partner is the person you go to for comfort. They represent unconditional love and are reaching for mutual goals with you, so it’s entirely natural to gravitate to this person when you need comfort or are dealing with any failure or disappointment.

When that person, your person, betrays you, that feeling of unconditional acceptance and love goes away. And because you no longer feel universally accepted by them, it’s infinitely more difficult to be vulnerable with them. So, instead of being transparent and raw with your partner, suddenly you have to be guarded.

You have to wonder if the news you’re about to share or the emotional breakdown that you’re on the verge of will be just one more thing that drives them away from you and into the arms of another. And to make matters worse, in the case of an affair, the person you usually go to for comfort is the very person who is causing you pain. That’s a difficult dynamic for your brain to understand and your heart to accept.

You don’t know who you are.

Couples tend to think of themselves as a unit. The “I” becomes “we” after you say, “I do,” and in many cases, long before that. Invitations are extended to you as a couple, and even your bank knows you as a unit. When one half of this singularity breaks the unity, you are left to identify as an individual again.

This is not to say that you’re automatically divorcing your spouse because of an affair, but this parting of the “we” in lieu of the “I” happens on an emotional level, long before divorce papers are ever served.

The point of marriage is to blend lives. Even the Bible tells us to become “one” with our spouse (Mark 10:6-9) and to abandon our singleness and, in some ways, the life we had prior to marriage. So, when something happens that loosens the glue that binds you together, you’re left with an identity crisis. “Who am I without them?” you might ask.

Blended lives are a beautiful thing, but when they fracture apart, the two individuals may find it more difficult to stand on their own than they did prior to the marriage.

You feel awkward.

Walking back into public life after an affair is a disorienting and awkward experience. You’re used to entering places in tandem and making decisions with the input of a partner. But now, you’re left to walk out into the world as a single. It shouldn’t be scary, right? You’ve done this before you were ever married. It shouldn’t be hard to be single again.

But you’re not the same young, somewhat naïve person you once were. You may not have the same youthful good looks or innocent charm to rely on that you once had, but you’re still you, whatever that means. You walk out into the world again, only this time, your confidence has been shaken, and you can’t seem to loosen this skepticism you feel that you will ever find anyone who thinks you’re worthy of love again.

You think that every eye is on you, whether they are judging, wondering, or even sympathizing. If you’ve been the victim of infidelity, you wonder if everyone knows, as if you’re wearing a scarlet letter on your sleeve.

You wonder if anyone finds you attractive or whether they ever will. After all, you’re older now, and those cute little glances and shy smiles you used to flash at prospective suitors don’t have the same effect. You wish that trick still worked on your spouse. You love them still, but you’re wondering if they love you.

Awkwardness and the self-awareness of your awkwardness can be overwhelming, not just to your mind, but also to your body. Your cheeks redden, and your heart begins to race, and you haven’t even gotten out of the car yet.

When you don’t know who you are and don’t particularly like what you think you are, it’s much more difficult to walk your daily life. Unfortunately, feeling awkward often leads to less than confident behavior, which might produce less than positive or enthusiastic responses from others. This then becomes a cycle where your fear of being awkward actually makes you, well, awkward.

Breaking Free

All these feelings that bloom out of infidelity can be overwhelming. They might feel as if they are permanent, that the damage is irreversible, and that you will never feel like yourself again. The good news is that infidelity, like every other human condition, is not too big or ominous for your Heavenly Father.

Through the power of the Holy Spirit, you can find that peace again. You can learn to trust and to feel confident, not because of the love and attention of a partner, but because you are a child of God. You can live a life that is full of joy and fulfillment, whether that means that you’re married or not. And perhaps most importantly, you can learn to forgive.

By laying out your heart to the Lord, reading Scripture, and seeking His face, you can find a path out of the insecurities and scars of infidelity into a new, more confident place. Maybe that means reconciling with your spouse. Maybe it means moving on in a different direction. God knows what’s best for you, and He wants to lead you to it.

Part of that healing process might include the guidance of a Christian therapist. A therapist can help you reconcile your feelings of betrayal and frame them in a way that you understand. They can help you learn to express yourself by giving you vocabulary and prompts that help you articulate your feelings, process them, and eventually move on from them.

A New Life

Infidelity doesn’t have to mean the end of your marriage, and certainly not the end of your life. You can recover from the battle scars of betrayal. You can forgive. You can reconcile. But you can also move on to a new life filled with possibilities and purpose.

It might be difficult to express or even understand the deep emotions you’re feeling right now, but with time, God’s guidance, and perhaps time with a professional counselor, you can start moving out of the fog and back into the light of God. Soon you will be walking confidently into the world, whether that’s alone or in a healed relationship.

Contact our office today to learn more and to schedule your first appointment with me or one of the other Christian counselors in our online directory.

item.title: Is It Possible for Kids to Control their Emotions? A Child Therapist Weighs In
item.description:
Upon asking if it is possible for kids to control their emotions, it is equally important to ask whether it is reasonable to expect it. As a therapist who has worked with children five years old and older, I will answer yes to both questions. Yes, it is possible for kids to control their emotions. And yes, it is reasonable to expect a child five years old to be able to control their emotions.

However, defining what that control means and looks like is key to understanding how it will look in operation and function in a child. Controlling emotions refers to the ability to identify, steward, and respond to emotional stimulation in a balanced or healthy way versus dismissing or ignoring them. Controlling emotions in therapeutic terms is referred to as emotional regulation.

Emotional regulation is the process of managing the intensity, duration, and expression of emotions to respond correctly to situations while maintaining mental well-being. Note that this definition does not intend for the child to avoid or repress the feelings that arise but requires them to manage their emotional reaction.

Emotional reaction management helps ensure that decision-making does not become overwhelmed and that social interactions remain mostly positive.

Every Child Can Learn About Emotions

Per the National Center for Education Statistics, children can learn more about their emotions than we sometimes give them credit for. Even young children are taking in information, remembering patterns, and beginning to connect what they feel with what is happening around them. By ages 2-3, children can begin holding on to information in meaningful ways.

As they move closer to ages 4-5, their memory, attention, and ability to follow simple steps continue to grow. This matters because emotional regulation is also learned step by step. A child may not always respond perfectly, but with consistent teaching, modeling, and practice, they can learn to pause, name what they feel, and choose a safer or more appropriate response.

Teaching children emotional regulation requires teaching them in a way they can comprehend. Children need the concept of “emotional regulation” broken down into a more understandable construct such as “pause and check in.” Often, taking the foundational meaning of words and using them with a younger mind helps them better connect with meaning.

Emotional regulation at its foundation is all about pausing and checking in with yourself first. Although emotional regulation is profoundly serious, allowing a child to learn emotional regulation by making it into a “tag-your-it” type of game is okay.

As a therapist who has worked with children and adolescents, the intensity can be lessened if fun can be had. However, always remind the child that fun is okay, and safety is the best friend of fun. We can have fun if you are safe, and so is everyone else. This is layered, but it is the step-by-step method that was previously mentioned. Once you convey the concept, begin to build on it to add other important ideas regarding emotional regulation.

What A Child Needs to Know About Their Emotions

The first thing that a child needs to know about their emotions is that they are not bad, stupid, make them an annoying person, make them weird, should make them feel scared, or any other negative conclusion they may have come to.

Children must know that emotions are a part of their human experience and their emotions are God given. The goal is to help them not only regulate their emotions but to understand them so that they can avoid shame or even embarrassment because of what they are feeling.

Here are a few simple phrases that can help children and adolescents feel seen, supported, and less alone in what they are experiencing.

  • “It’s okay to not feel okay.” – Normalizes odd feelings without judgement.
  • “Sadness can feel lonely. Can I sit with you quietly?” – Normalize maintaining connecting during tough times versus isolation.
  • “Crying is okay. I will get you some tissue.” – The focus is getting the child comfortable with being supported while being validated (seen).
  • “Feeling scared is hard. What do you need right now? – The focus is getting the child to speak to how to name what would meet their need, by using their words.

The key is to keep it simple, continue step-by-step and to model. Children need to see that we not only understand but are present. Being present is not just about our bodies being in the same space, meaning proximity. They need to know that an adult is present in their eyes and with their hearts. This matters to any child in any emotional state at any time.

Modeling is one of the most effective ways children learn emotional regulation. Children are always watching how the adults around them respond to frustration, sadness, disappointment, fear, and even joy.

When adults can slow down, name what is happening, and respond steadily, children begin to learn that emotions can be felt without taking over the whole moment. This is not about being perfect in front of a child. It is about allowing the child to see regulation practiced in real time.

One Step Further

The goal is to build a foundation of understanding not only emotional regulation but to also take it one step further to begin establishing good mental health. Think about that for a second, what if it was widespread practice to put into place the building blocks for children to have a good headstart to sound mental health.

Children who understand their emotions grow into adults who understand their emotions as well as how to manage them. Children can control their emotions when they learn that their emotions are a part of their human experience.

As a therapist who is a Christian, I can tell you that unpacking that truth, along with the reality that God equipped us with emotions for a purpose, and that they are good. God speaks of emotions and how to manage them throughout His Word.

A child must know that anger is real and God is aware. Fear is going to show up; God knew it and warned us that we were going to have to stand up to fear, not run from it. With God’s help, they can emotionally regulate.

Children are easy to teach when we know what we are teaching and how to teach it. When controlling emotions is taught with consideration of self, others, environment, and outcome, it helps to create step-by-step instruction, which creates consistency in demonstration and modeling.

As children grow into adolescents the emotional lessons that they learn will undoubtedly stick with them while allowing additional knowledge of more complicated emotional concepts.

Sensitivity can be learned, and due to our culture, which is heavily packed with less-kind television programming, video games, and movie entertainment, sensitivity is an emotion we cannot afford to leave children to gather on their own.

Teaching children how to manage anger and express it in a healthy way is a necessity our current society can no longer ignore. Ignoring emotional health until it becomes a crisis. When a child is in mental crisis, there is less chance of helping them, and it is harder to assist the appointed adult with comprehending what is happening with them in the moment.

The more clarity that can be given to children to help them identify and understand their emotions, the better we can help them manage what they go through while continuing to understand who they are and will become emotionally.

item.title: Bible Verses for Overeating Disorder
item.description:
Is overeating a struggle for you? Many of us face this struggle daily in our abundant culture, where food is tempting and readily available. However, the Bible can help you have better health by reminding you to curb your overeating habits.

When you use specific verses of God’s Word to prepare yourself, you can fight back with confidence when you are tempted to overeat. Jesus used Scripture to fight temptation at a time when he was very hungry (Matt. 4:1-11). If he did this to overcome Satan, we can do the same thing to gain spiritual victory.

The following verses are powerful weapons for you to fight temptation. Meditate on them, memorize them, write them down, post them where you see them often, and save them to your phone. The more ways you hide God’s Word in your heart, the more easily you will remember it when you are tempted to overeat. You can ask the Holy Spirit to bring them to mind when you need accountability in your eating habits.

The Best Bible Verses for Overeating Disorder

You can turn each of the following verses into a prayer in times of temptation. God will meet you right in those moments and give you the strength to overcome. He promises to deliver you from whatever temptation you face, and he will empower you to make better choices for your health.

…the rules of the Lord are true, and righteous altogether. More to be desired are they than gold, even much fine gold; sweeter also than honey and drippings of the honeycomb. – Psalm 19:9b-10

God considers his laws to be more desirable than the sweetest food available during Bible times – honey. His laws are more desirable than the finest gold, or perhaps your food craving of choice: chips, French fries, doughnuts, ice cream, pizza, or whatever tempts you most.

Remember that when you follow God’s laws, you will be blessed with a clean conscience. You won’t be riddled with guilt and shame like you may be when you overeat. God will help you make wise eating choices so you can live a disciplined life for his Kingdom work. His laws lead to life, while our poor choices lead to destruction, so remember this verse when you are tempted.

So I will bless you as long as I live; in your name I will lift up my hands. My soul will be satisfied as with fat and rich food, and my mouth will praise you with joyful lips. – Psalm 63:4-5

What are the richest foods you have tasted? Steak, lobster, cheesecake, or something else? Are you honestly as satisfied with God as you are when you eat these rich foods? You can learn to be more satisfied with God’s presence than you are with food, though this will take discipline.

The peace you find in God’s presence lasts much longer than the pleasure you get from eating rich food. When you learn to gain your true satisfaction from God, your faith will be grounded even while food looks tempting to you.

Delight yourself in the Lord, and he will give you the desires of your heart. – Psalm 37:4

What are the desires of your heart when you are tempted to overeat? It’s probably not to simply feel full or enjoy the taste and texture of food. Most of us overeat to soothe our emotions and fill a place inside that feels empty. Often people with overeating disorders deal with loneliness, rejection, anxiety, depression, and other problems.

A caring Christian counselor can help you get to the roots of why you overeat. You can learn that taking delight in the Lord is much more satisfying than overeating, and you can trust him with the deepest desires of your heart.

How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth! – Psalm 119:103

God’s Word will become sweeter to you the more you meditate on it, study it, and apply it to your life. The Bible has healing properties, just like real honey does. But God’s Word heals you with God’s love, comfort, encouragement, protection, and joy as you learn to relax in his presence and enjoy time with him. Each day, meet with God for a few minutes, asking him to make his words sweeter than honey to you and healing for your soul.

Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth; keep watch over the door of my lips! Do not let my heart incline to any evil, to busy myself with wicked deeds in company with men who work iniquity, and let me not eat of their delicacies! – Psalm 141:3-4

These verses address the issue of controlling what we say. But they can also apply to what food passes over our lips. We can ask God to stand guard over our lips when we are faced with a tempting situation.

He will help you stop putting things into your mouth that aren’t good for you. You can ask God to keep you from drifting toward evil choices and help you avoid the wrong kinds of delicacies. The next time you are tempted, simply pray “Guard my lips,” and God will be right beside you.

I cry to you, O Lord; I say, “You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living.” – Psalm 142:5

When you feel like you want that third piece of cake or fourth slice of pizza, you can pray this verse. You can say, “Lord, I think I want this food right now. But I know my true craving should be for you because you alone can satisfy me.” Then walk away from the temptation, drink a glass of water, and engage in a different activity. God will be your refuge in that moment, a haven where you can find comfort that lasts longer than the food you are craving.

If you have found honey, eat only enough for you, lest you have your fill of it and vomit it. – Proverbs 25:16

The Bible is eminently practical. Any food, even healthy food like honey, can make you sick if you overeat. Choose to eat a balanced diet of nourishing foods to protect your health and feel your best. When you are tempted to overeat in certain food categories, remember this verse and don’t succumb to temptation.

Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” – Matthew 26:41

Our minds and spirits may be willing to make wise food choices, but the sinful nature of our flesh is vulnerable to temptation. All of us face this scenario at one time or another, particularly when we are stressed. But God will help you in the very moment of temptation if you cry out to him. Admit to him that your flesh is weak, and ask him to deliver you from the temptation to overeat.

No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation, he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it. – 1 Corinthians 10:13

This verse can be a practical comfort to you in times of temptation. Ask God to provide you a way out when you are about to overeat. He might instruct you to remove tempting foods from your pantry or eat a mini-meal before going to a restaurant. You can form more practical strategies to serve as escape routes with a qualified Christian counselor.

Christian Counseling for Overeating

The roots of overeating run deep for most people. You may need help from a Christian counselor to overcome overeating disorder. A counselor will offer Bible-based care with compassion and understanding. Your counselor will encourage you with principles that can keep you on track for a healthier lifestyle.
